title: HTML & CSS
summary: Build real web pages from scratch: structure content with semantic HTML, then style and lay it out with modern CSS, flexbox, grid and responsive, accessible design.

lessons.title: How the web works and page structure
lessons.summary: Understand what HTML and CSS do and write the skeleton every web page needs.

slides.title: Three languages of the web
slides.text:
- **HTML**: the content and its structure
- **CSS**: how it looks
- **JavaScript**: how it behaves
slides.narration:
Every web page you have ever seen is built from three languages working together.
HTML describes the content, like headings, paragraphs and images. CSS decides how it looks: colors, fonts and layout. JavaScript adds behavior.
In this course we master the first two.

slides.title: Tags and elements
slides.text:
HTML uses **tags** in angle brackets.
Opening tag + content + closing tag = an **element**.
slides.code:
This is a paragraph.

Important!
slides.narration:
HTML is made of elements. Most have an opening tag, some content, and a closing tag with a slash.
A few, like img, are empty elements with no closing tag.
Extra information goes in attributes, like src and alt, written inside the opening tag.

slides.title: The page skeleton
slides.text: Every page starts with the same structure.
slides.code: Hello, web!
slides.narration:
Here is the skeleton of every web page. The doctype tells the browser this is modern HTML.
The head holds information about the page, like its title and character set. The body holds everything visible.

slides.title: Nesting and indentation
slides.text:
Elements live **inside** other elements, like boxes in boxes.
Close them in the **reverse** order you opened them.
slides.code:
I really like HTML.

I really
slides.narration:
Elements nest inside each other. The element you opened last must be closed first.
Indent nested elements so the structure is easy to see. And notice the comment syntax, which starts with less than, exclamation mark and two dashes.

slides.title: Previewing your page
slides.text:
Write HTML in the editor and press **Run** to see it in the preview.
The browser is **forgiving**: it shows something even with mistakes, so check carefully.
slides.narration:
In Averroes Code, press Run to preview your page.
Browsers try hard to display broken HTML, which means mistakes do not always cause visible errors. Keep your code tidy and check it often.

Hello, web!

This is my first web page. I built it in Averroes Code.

Today I learned that HTML describes structure, and CSS describes style.

quiz.q: Which language controls how a page looks?
quiz.explain: CSS is responsible for presentation: colors, fonts and layout.

quiz.q: Where does the visible content of a page go?
quiz.explain: Everything shown in the page goes inside <body>.

quiz.q: Which is correctly nested?
quiz.explain: The last opened element (<b>) must be closed first.

lessons.task:
Create your first page:

1. Write the full skeleton (`<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<html lang="en">`, `<head>`, `<body>`).
2. Give it the title `About me`.
3. In the body add a heading `<h1>` with your name and two paragraphs about yourself.
4. Add one HTML comment explaining what the page is.
5. Press Run and check that the title appears and everything is correctly nested.

lessons.title: Headings, paragraphs and text
lessons.summary: Structure text with headings, paragraphs, line breaks and inline elements for emphasis.

slides.title: Headings h1 to h6
slides.text:
Six levels: `<h1>` most important, `<h6>` least.
Use **one** `<h1>` per page and do not skip levels.
slides.code:
Cooking Basics

Knife skills

Holding the knife
slides.narration:
Headings create the outline of your page, like chapters and sections in a book.
There are six levels. Use one h1 for the main title, then h2 for sections, h3 for sub sections, and so on.
Choose headings for their meaning, not their size. CSS can change the size later.

slides.title: Paragraphs and breaks
slides.text:
`

` for paragraphs. `
` for a line break **inside** text. `

` for a topic change.
slides.code:
HTML ignores extra spaces and line breaks in your code.

Roses are red,
violets are blue.
slides.narration:
Each paragraph goes in its own p element.
The browser collapses extra spaces and line breaks into a single space, so use br when you really need a line break, like in a poem or an address.

slides.title: Emphasis and meaning
slides.text:
- `<strong>` important
- `<em>` stressed emphasis
- `<mark>` highlighted
- `<code>` code
slides.code:
Warning: the oven is very hot.

Run npm install first.

The answer is 42.
slides.narration:
Inline elements add meaning to words inside a paragraph.
strong marks something important, em adds stress, mark highlights, and code shows computer code.
Screen readers can use this meaning, which is why we prefer them over purely visual tags.

slides.title: Quotes and special characters
slides.text:
`<blockquote>` and `<q>` for quotes.
**Entities** for reserved characters: `<` `>` `&` `©`
slides.code:
Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability.

Use <p> for paragraphs. © 2026
slides.narration:
For longer quotes use blockquote, for short inline quotes use q.
Since less than and greater than signs start tags, write them as entities when you want to show them as text, like ampersand l t semicolon.

quiz.q: How many <h1> elements should a typical page have?
quiz.explain: One h1 describes the page; sections use h2 and below.

quiz.q: What does the browser do with several spaces in a row in HTML text?
quiz.explain: Whitespace is collapsed unless you use <pre> or CSS white-space.

quiz.q: How do you display a literal < in text?
quiz.explain: < is the entity for the less-than sign.

lessons.task:
Write a short article page about a hobby:

1. One `<h1>` title, at least two `<h2>` sections, and one `<h3>` inside a section.
2. At least three paragraphs using `<strong>`, `<em>` and `<code>` or `<kbd>`.
3. A `<blockquote>` with a quote you like.
4. Show the text `<html>` literally on the page using entities.
5. Check that your heading levels never skip a level.

lessons.title: Links and images
lessons.summary: Connect pages with links and add images with good alt text and sensible sizes.

slides.title: The anchor element
slides.text: `<a href="...">` makes a **hyperlink**: the "hyper" in HTML.
slides.code: MDN Web Docs About us Jump to contact
slides.narration:
Links are what make the web a web. The a element, called an anchor, uses the href attribute to say where to go.
It can point to another website, another file in your project, or a section of the same page using a hash and an id.

slides.title: Absolute and relative paths
slides.text:
- **Absolute**: full URL `https://site.com/page`
- **Relative**: from the current file `img/logo.png`, `../index.html`
slides.code: Home Team (same folder)
slides.narration:
Absolute links include the full address. Relative links describe a path from the current file.
Two dots mean go up one folder. Use relative links between pages of your own site so it still works when you move it.

slides.title: More link tricks
slides.text:
- `target="_blank"` opens a new tab
- `mailto:` and `tel:` links
- Link text should **describe** the destination
slides.code: Example (new tab) Email us Call us
slides.narration:
target blank opens the link in a new tab. Pair it with rel noopener for safety.
mailto and tel links open the email app or the phone dialer.
And always write meaningful link text. Click here tells a screen reader user nothing.

slides.title: Images
slides.text: `` **alt** describes the image for people who cannot see it.
slides.narration:
The img element shows a picture. src is the file path, and alt is a text description.
Alt text is read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Width and height let the browser reserve space so the page does not jump.

slides.title: Figures and formats
slides.text:
`<figure>` + `<figcaption>` for captioned images.
Formats: **JPEG** photos, **PNG** sharp graphics, **SVG** icons, **WebP/AVIF** modern and small.
slides.narration:
When an image needs a caption, wrap it in figure and add a figcaption.
Pick the right format: JPEG for photos, PNG for sharp graphics, SVG for icons and logos, and WebP or AVIF for small modern files.

lessons.notes: ## Links ```html W3C Contact First post Home FAQ Email Download CV ``` - Opening in a new tab: `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"`. Use it sparingly; users can choose themselves. - Link text must make sense out of context: "Read the pricing guide", not "click here". - Any element with an `id` can be a link target. ## Images ```html ``` | Attribute | Purpose | |---|---| | `src` | path or URL of the image | | `alt` | text alternative (required) | | `width` / `height` | intrinsic size; prevents layout jumps | | `loading="lazy"` | load only when near the screen | **Writing alt text:** describe the information the image gives, in context. Decorative images get an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip them. Do not start with "image of". ## Captions ```html ``` ## Responsive images (preview) ```html ``` The browser picks the best file for the screen. We return to this in the responsive design lesson. ## Image formats JPEG (photos), PNG (transparency, screenshots), SVG (vector logos and icons that scale perfectly), WebP and AVIF (modern, much smaller files, supported by all current browsers).

lessons.task:
Build a two-page mini site in one folder:

1. `index.html` with a heading, a paragraph and a link to `about.html`.
2. `about.html` with a link back to `index.html`.
3. On `index.html`, add an image inside a `<figure>` with a meaningful `alt`, `width`, `height` and a `<figcaption>`.

lessons.title: Lists and tables
lessons.summary: Organize content with unordered, ordered and description lists, and present data in accessible tables.

slides.title: Unordered and ordered lists
slides.text:
- `<ul>` bullets, order does not matter
- `<ol>` numbers, order matters
- Each item is an `<li>`
slides.code:
• Milk
  • Bread
  1. Preheat oven
  2. Bake 20 minutes
slides.narration:
Lists are everywhere: shopping lists, steps in a recipe, navigation menus.
Use ul when the order does not matter, and ol when it does. Every item goes inside an li element.

slides.title: Nested and description lists
slides.text: Lists can contain lists. `<dl>` pairs **terms** and **descriptions**.
slides.code:
• Fruit
    • Apple
    • Kiwi
HTML
Structure of a page
CSS
Style of a page
slides.narration:
You can put a whole list inside a list item to create sub lists.
A description list, dl, is perfect for glossaries and key value pairs: dt is the term, dd is its description.

slides.title: Table basics
slides.text:
Tables are for **tabular data**: rows and columns.
`<table>` > `<tr>` rows > `<th>` headers / `<td>` cells
slides.code:
PlanetMoons
Earth1
Mars2
slides.narration:
Use a table whenever your data naturally has rows and columns, like a timetable or a price list.
Each row is a t r element. Header cells use t h and normal cells use t d.

slides.title: Accessible tables
slides.text:
- `<caption>` titles the table
- `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `<tfoot>` group rows
- `scope="col"` / `scope="row"` link headers to cells
slides.code:
Monthly budget
ItemCost
Rent$800
slides.narration:
Give every table a caption. Group the rows into a head, body and foot.
The scope attribute tells screen readers whether a header describes a column or a row, so each cell can be announced with its headers.

slides.title: Merging cells
slides.text:
`colspan` and `rowspan` stretch a cell across columns or rows.
**Never** use tables for page layout. That is CSS's job.
slides.code: Total: $950
slides.narration:
colspan makes a cell span several columns, and rowspan spans several rows.
One rule: tables are only for data. Long ago people used them to lay out whole pages, but today we use CSS flexbox and grid for layout.

quiz.q: Which list should you use for step-by-step instructions?
quiz.explain: The order matters for steps, so use an ordered list.

quiz.q: Which element is a header cell in a table?
quiz.explain: <th> marks a header cell; <thead> groups header rows.

quiz.q: What should tables NOT be used for?
quiz.explain: Tables are for tabular data. Layout is done with CSS.

lessons.task:
Make a "My week" page:

1. An ordered list of your morning routine (at least 4 steps).
2. An unordered list of hobbies, with one nested sub-list.
3. A description list with three terms you learned in this course.
4. A timetable `<table>` with a `<caption>`, `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `scope` attributes and at least one cell using `colspan`.
5. Add simple CSS borders so the table is readable.

lessons.title: Forms and inputs
lessons.summary: Collect user input with forms, labels, input types, select menus, buttons and built-in validation.

slides.title: What forms do
slides.text:
Forms collect data: logins, searches, sign-ups, orders.
`<form action method>` wraps the controls.
slides.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email">
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
slides.narration:
Forms are how users talk back to a website.
The form element wraps the controls. action says where to send the data, and method says how: get for searches, post for sending private or changing data.
Each control needs a name, which becomes the key in the submitted data.

slides.title: Labels are essential
slides.text: Every input needs a `<label>`. Link them with `for` and `id`.
slides.code:
<label for="name">Full name</label>
<input id="name" name="name" type="text">

<label><input type="checkbox" name="terms"> I agree</label>
slides.narration:
Every control needs a visible label. Connect them by giving the input an id and the label a matching for attribute, or by putting the input inside the label.
Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers announce it correctly.

slides.title: Input types
slides.text: `text` `email` `password` `number` `date` `tel` `url` `search` `range` `color` `checkbox` `radio` `file`
slides.code:
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">
<input type="date">
<input type="radio" name="size" value="s" id="s"><label for="s">Small</label>
<input type="radio" name="size" value="l" id="l"><label for="l">Large</label>
slides.narration:
The type attribute changes the control and the keyboard shown on phones.
Radio buttons with the same name form a group where only one can be chosen. Checkboxes allow several choices.

slides.title: Selects, textareas and buttons
slides.text:
- `<select>` + `<option>` dropdown
- `<textarea>` multi-line text
- `<button type="submit|button|reset">`
slides.code:
<select name="country">
  <option value="">Choose...</option>
  <option value="eg">Egypt</option>
</select>
<textarea name="message" rows="4"></textarea>
<button type="submit">Send</button>
slides.narration:
A select element makes a dropdown of options. A textarea accepts several lines of text.
Buttons inside a form submit it by default, so give other buttons type button.

slides.title: Built-in validation
slides.text:
`required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max`, `pattern`
The browser checks **before** sending.
slides.code:
<input name="user" required minlength="3">
<input name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="5 digits">
<input name="age" type="number" min="13">
slides.narration:
HTML can check input for you. required means the field cannot be empty, and attributes like minlength, min and pattern set rules.
The browser shows a message and blocks sending until the rules are met. Servers must still check data again, because users can bypass the browser.

slides.title: Grouping fields
slides.text: `<fieldset>` + `<legend>` group related controls.
slides.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="d" value="std"> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="d" value="exp"> Express</label>
</fieldset>
slides.narration:
For bigger forms, group related fields in a fieldset with a legend as its title.
It is especially important for radio groups, because the legend explains what the choice is about.

lessons.notes:
## The form element

```html
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="q">Search</label>
  <input id="q" name="q" type="search" placeholder="e.g. flexbox">
  <button>Go</button>
</form>
```

- `method="get"` puts data in the URL (`/search?q=flexbox`): good for searches.
- `method="post"` sends data in the request body: use it for logins and anything that changes data.
- Only controls with a `name` are submitted.

## Labels

```html
<label for="pw">Password</label>
<input id="pw" name="pw" type="password" autocomplete="current-password">
```

A `placeholder` is **not** a label: it disappears when typing and often has low contrast.

## Common input types

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| `text`, `search` | free text |
| `email`, `url`, `tel` | validated / mobile keyboard |
| `password` | hidden characters |
| `number`, `range` | numbers (with `min`, `max`, `step`) |
| `date`, `time` | date and time pickers |
| `checkbox` | several independent choices |
| `radio` | one choice from a group (same `name`) |
| `file` | uploads (form needs `enctype="multipart/form-data"`) |
| `color` | color picker |

## Other controls

`<select>` with `<option>` (and `<optgroup>`), `<textarea>`, `<datalist>` for suggestions, `<output>`, `<progress>`.

## Validation attributes

`required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max`, `step`, `pattern`. CSS can style states with `:valid`, `:invalid` and `:user-invalid` (only after the user interacts).

**Security note:** browser validation improves the experience but is never security. Always validate again on the server.

## Helpful extras

- `autocomplete="email"`, `"name"`, `"new-password"` help browsers fill forms.
- `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` group related fields.
- `disabled` and `readonly` prevent editing (disabled fields are not submitted).

quiz.explain: The label's for attribute must match the input's id.

quiz.q: Several radio buttons form one group when they share the same...
quiz.explain: Radio buttons with the same name are mutually exclusive.

quiz.q: Is browser validation enough to keep bad data out of a server?
options: No, the server must validate too
quiz.explain: Users can bypass the browser, so servers must always validate.

lessons.task:
Build a "Book a table" form for a restaurant:

1. Fields: name (required), email (type `email`, required), phone (`tel`), date (`date`), number of guests (`number`, 1 to 12).
2. A radio group in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`: indoor / outdoor.
3. A `<select>` for the time and a `<textarea>` for special requests.
4. Every control must have a connected `<label>`.
5. Try submitting empty and invalid values and watch the browser's validation messages.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.summary: Use header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer so pages have meaning, not just looks.

slides.title: Meaning over appearance
slides.text:
**Semantic** elements say **what** content is.
`<div>` and `<span>` say nothing.
slides.code:
...
...
slides.narration:
Semantic means meaningful. A div is a generic box that says nothing about its content.
Elements like header and nav tell the browser, search engines and screen readers exactly what each part of the page is.

slides.title: Page landmarks
slides.text: `<header>` `<nav>` `<main>` `<aside>` `<footer>`
slides.code:
<body>
  <header>Logo + site title</header>
  <nav>Main menu</nav>
  <main>Unique page content</main>
  <aside>Related links</aside>
  <footer>Copyright, contacts</footer>
</body>
slides.narration:
These five elements are landmarks. Screen reader users can jump straight to them, like chapters.
Use exactly one main per page, for the content that is unique to that page.

slides.title: article and section
slides.text:
- `<article>`: complete, standalone content (a post, a card)
- `<section>`: a themed part of a page, usually with a heading
slides.code:
How I learned CSS

...

The box model
slides.narration:
An article is something that makes sense on its own, like a blog post or a product card.
A section groups related content inside a page or article, and should usually start with a heading.

slides.title: div and span still matter
slides.text: Use `<div>` (block) and `<span>` (inline) **only** when no semantic element fits, usually for styling.
slides.code:
Price: $12

...
slides.narration:
div and span are not bad. They are the right choice when you only need a hook for CSS and no semantic element fits.
Just reach for a meaningful element first.

lessons.notes:

` is easier to read than `

1. A `<header>` with your name and a `<nav>` list of links.
2. A `<main>` with at least two `<section>` elements, each with a heading.

lessons.title: CSS basics and selectors
lessons.summary: Add CSS to a page, write rules, target elements with selectors and understand the cascade and specificity.

slides.title: Anatomy of a CSS rule
slides.text: **selector** { **property**: **value**; }
slides.narration:
CSS is a list of rules. Each rule has a selector that picks elements, and a block of declarations.
Each declaration is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon. Here, every h1 becomes navy and two rem tall.

slides.title: Where CSS lives
slides.text:
1. **External file** (best): `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`
2. `<style>` in the head
3. Inline `style="..."` (avoid)
slides.code:
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
  <style>
    p { line-height: 1.6; }
  </style>
</head>
slides.narration:
The best place for CSS is a separate file linked from the head, so many pages can share it.
A style element is fine for small examples, which is what we use in this course. Inline styles are hard to maintain, so avoid them.

slides.title: Basic selectors
slides.text:
- `p` type
- `.card` class
- `#main` id
- `*` everything
- `h1, h2` group
slides.narration:
The type selector targets every element of a kind. A dot selects a class, which you can reuse on many elements. A hash selects a single id.
Separate selectors with commas to apply one rule to several of them.

slides.title: Combinators and pseudo-classes
slides.text:
- `nav a` descendant, `ul > li` child
- `a:hover`, `input:focus`, `li:first-child`, `li:nth-child(odd)`
slides.narration:
Combinators target elements by their position. A space means anywhere inside, and the greater than sign means direct child.
Pseudo classes, starting with a colon, target states like hover and focus, or positions like first child.

slides.title: The cascade and specificity
slides.text:
When rules conflict:
1. More **specific** selector wins (id > class > type)
2. If equal, the **later** rule wins
slides.code:
p { color: black; }        /* 0-0-1 */
.note { color: green; }    /* 0-1-0 wins */
p { color: red; }          /* later, but less specific */
slides.narration:
Cascading is the C in CSS. When two rules set the same property, the more specific selector wins. An id beats a class, and a class beats a type.
If they are equally specific, the one that comes later wins. Keep specificity low by mostly using classes.

slides.title: Inheritance
slides.text:
Text properties (color, font) **inherit** from parents.
Box properties (border, margin) do **not**.
slides.narration:
Some properties pass down from parent to children automatically. Set the font and text color on body once, and the whole page follows.
Borders, margins and backgrounds do not inherit, which is usually what you want.

lessons.task:
Style your semantic "About me" page:

1. Move all styles into a `<style>` block (or `style.css` linked in the head).
2. Set the font and text color once on `body`.
3. Use at least one type, one class, one id, one descendant and one child selector.

5. Create a conflict on purpose and use the browser's Inspect tool to see which rule wins and why.

lessons.title: Colors, units and typography
lessons.summary: Use color formats, CSS custom properties, units like rem and %, and style text with fonts.

slides.title: Color formats
slides.narration:
CSS understands many color formats. Hex codes are the most common in design files.
rgb mixes red, green and blue, and the slash adds transparency. hsl uses hue, saturation and lightness, which is easy to tweak by hand.

slides.title: Custom properties (variables)
slides.text: Define once in `:root`, use with `var()`.
slides.narration:
Custom properties are CSS variables. Their names start with two dashes, and you read them with var.
Put your colors in one place, and changing your whole theme becomes a one line edit.

slides.title: Units
slides.text:
- `px` fixed pixels
- `rem` relative to the root font size (great for text and spacing)
- `em` relative to the current font size
- `%`, `vw`, `vh` relative to container / viewport
slides.narration:
Sizes need units. Pixels are fixed. rem is relative to the root font size, so if a user increases their browser text size, your layout grows with it.
Percent, v w and v h are relative to the parent or the screen.

slides.title: Fonts
slides.text: `font-family` with **fallbacks**, `font-size`, `font-weight`, `line-height`
slides.narration:
font family takes a list. If the first font is missing, the browser tries the next, ending with a generic family like sans serif.
A line height around one point five makes body text much easier to read.

slides.title: Text styling
slides.text: `text-align`, `text-decoration`, `text-transform`, `max-width` for readable lines
slides.narration:
Long lines are tiring to read. Limit text width to about sixty five characters with the ch unit.
Text align, transform and decoration control alignment, capitals and underlines.

quiz.q: How do you use a custom property named --brand?
quiz.explain: Custom properties are read with var().

quiz.q: Which unit is relative to the root (html) font size?

quiz.q: Why list several fonts in font-family?
options: As fallbacks if a font is unavailable
quiz.explain: The browser uses the first available font in the list.

lessons.task:
Create a theme for your site:

1. Define at least four custom properties in `:root` (brand color, text, background, spacing).
2. Use `var()` everywhere instead of repeating raw values.
3. Set a font stack with a generic fallback, `line-height` of about 1.5, and limit text width with `ch`.
4. Use `rem` for font sizes and spacing.
5. Bonus: add a `prefers-color-scheme: dark` media query that changes only the custom properties.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.summary: Understand content, padding, border and margin, box-sizing, display types and overflow.

slides.title: Everything is a box
slides.text:
Every element is a rectangle made of:
**content** → **padding** → **border** → **margin**
slides.narration:
Here is the most important idea in CSS layout: every element is a box.
In the middle is the content. Around it is padding, the inner space. Then the border. And outside the border, margin, the space that pushes other boxes away.

slides.title: box-sizing: border-box
slides.text: By default `width` is **content only**. With `border-box`, width **includes** padding and border.
slides.narration:
By default, padding and border are added on top of the width, which makes sizes confusing.
Setting box sizing to border box everywhere makes the width you write the width you get. Almost every modern stylesheet starts with this rule.

slides.title: Shorthands
slides.text:
`margin: top right bottom left` (clockwise)
`margin: 10px 20px` = vertical horizontal
`margin: 0 auto` centers a block
slides.narration:
Margin and padding accept one to four values, going clockwise from the top: top, right, bottom, left.
Two values mean vertical and horizontal. A left and right margin of auto centers a block that has a width.

slides.title: Block vs inline
slides.text:
- **block**: new line, full width (`div`, `p`, `h1`)
- **inline**: flows in text, ignores width/height (`span`, `a`)
- **inline-block**: inline, but accepts size
slides.narration:
The display property decides how a box behaves. Block boxes start on a new line and take the full width. Inline boxes flow inside text.
inline block flows like text but respects width and padding, which is perfect for buttons. display none removes an element completely.

slides.title: Margin collapse and overflow
slides.text:
- Vertical margins between blocks **collapse** (the larger wins)
- `overflow: auto` adds scrollbars when content is too big
slides.narration:
A surprising rule: when two vertical margins touch, they collapse into one, the larger of the two.
And when content is bigger than its box, overflow decides whether it spills out, is clipped, or gets scrollbars.

lessons.notes:
## The four layers

```
+------------------- margin -------------------+
|  +--------------- border ----------------+   |
|  |  +----------- padding ------------+   |   |
|  |  |           content              |   |   |
|  |  +--------------------------------+   |   |
|  +---------------------------------------+   |
+-----------------------------------------------+
```

- **padding**: space inside the border; the background shows here.
- **border**: `border: 2px solid #333;`, `border-radius` rounds corners.
- **margin**: transparent space outside; can be negative or `auto`.

## box-sizing

```css
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
```

With the default `content-box`, a `width: 300px` box with `padding: 20px` and `border: 5px` is actually 350px wide. With `border-box` it is 300px.

## Shorthand values

| Values | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `10px` | all sides |
| `10px 20px` | top/bottom, left/right |
| `10px 20px 30px` | top, left/right, bottom |
| `10px 20px 30px 40px` | top, right, bottom, left |

Logical properties like `margin-inline` and `padding-block` adapt to right-to-left languages such as Arabic.

## Display

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `block` | own line, full width, respects width/height |
| `inline` | flows in text; width/height ignored |
| `inline-block` | flows in text but respects size |
| `none` | removed from the page |
| `flex` / `grid` | layout containers (next lessons) |

## Sizing

`width`, `max-width`, `min-height`, `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9`. Prefer `max-width` over fixed `width` so boxes can shrink on small screens.

## Margin collapsing and overflow

Adjacent vertical margins of block elements merge into the larger one. It does not happen inside flex or grid containers.

`overflow: visible | hidden | scroll | auto` controls content that does not fit.

## Debugging tip

Temporarily add `outline: 1px solid red;` to see box edges without changing the layout, or use the box model diagram in the browser's Inspect panel.

Build a "profile card":

1. Add the `border-box` reset at the top of your CSS.
2. Create a card with `max-width: 320px`, centered with `margin: 0 auto`.
3. Give it padding, a border, rounded corners and a shadow (`box-shadow`).

lessons.title: Flexbox layout
lessons.summary: Arrange items in a row or column, align them and distribute space with flexbox.

slides.title: One-dimensional layout
slides.text: `display: flex` on a **container** lines its children up in a row (or column).
slides.narration:
Flexbox is a layout system for arranging items in one direction, a row or a column.
Put display flex on the parent, called the flex container, and its direct children become flex items lined up in a row. gap adds space between them.

slides.title: Direction and wrapping
slides.text:
- `flex-direction: row | column`
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items move to the next line
slides.code:
.stack { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.tags  { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem; }
slides.narration:
flex direction switches between a row and a column. The direction you choose is the main axis, and the other is the cross axis.
By default items squeeze onto one line. flex wrap lets them flow onto new lines.

slides.title: justify-content
slides.text:
Aligns items along the **main axis**.
`flex-start` `center` `flex-end` `space-between` `space-around` `space-evenly`
slides.narration:
justify content distributes items along the main axis.
space between is a classic for navigation bars: the logo on the left, the menu on the right, and all the free space in between.

slides.title: align-items
slides.text:
Aligns items on the **cross axis**.
`stretch` (default) `center` `flex-start` `flex-end` `baseline`
slides.narration:
align items controls the other direction, the cross axis.
Combine justify content center with align items center and you have the famous perfect centering trick, which used to be very hard in CSS.

slides.title: Flexible sizes
slides.text:
`flex: grow shrink basis`
`flex: 1` = share space equally
slides.code:
.sidebar { flex: 0 0 250px; } /* fixed 250px */
.content { flex: 1; }         /* take the rest */
.card    { flex: 1 1 200px; } /* at least ~200px, then grow */
slides.narration:
The flex property on items controls how they grow and shrink.
flex one means take an equal share of the free space. A sidebar with flex zero zero two fifty pixels stays fixed while the content fills the rest.

lessons.notes:
## Container and items

```css
.container {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row;        /* row | row-reverse | column | column-reverse */
  flex-wrap: wrap;            /* nowrap (default) | wrap */
  justify-content: center;    /* main axis */
  align-items: center;        /* cross axis */
  gap: 1rem;                  /* space between items */
}
```

Only **direct children** become flex items.

## Axes

- **Main axis**: the direction of `flex-direction` (horizontal for `row`).
- **Cross axis**: perpendicular to it.
- `justify-content` works on the main axis, `align-items` on the cross axis. With `flex-direction: column` they swap visually.

## justify-content values

| Value | Result |
|---|---|
| `flex-start` | packed at the start |
| `center` | centered |
| `flex-end` | packed at the end |
| `space-between` | first and last at the edges, equal gaps between |
| `space-around` | equal space around each item |
| `space-evenly` | perfectly equal gaps everywhere |

## Item properties

```css
.item {
  flex: 1 1 200px;     /* grow, shrink, basis */
  align-self: flex-end; /* override align-items for one item */
  order: 2;             /* visual order (use carefully, see a11y) */
}
```

- `flex: 1` share free space equally.
- `flex: none` keep natural size.
- `margin-left: auto` on one item pushes it (and the rest) to the far end, handy in navbars.

## Typical uses

- Navigation bars, toolbars, button groups.
- Centering anything.
- Cards that wrap onto new lines (`flex-wrap: wrap` + `flex: 1 1 250px`).
- Sticky footer: `body { display: flex; flex-direction: column; min-height: 100vh } main { flex: 1 }`.

Use **flexbox** for one-dimensional layouts (a row or a column) and **grid** for two-dimensional layouts (rows and columns together).

quiz.q: Where do you write display: flex?
quiz.explain: display: flex goes on the container; its direct children become flex items.

quiz.q: Which property aligns items along the main axis?
quiz.explain: justify-content distributes items along the main axis.

quiz.q: What does flex: 1 on every item do?
quiz.explain: Each item grows equally to fill the available space.

lessons.task:
Build a responsive header and feature row with flexbox:

1. A navbar: logo on the left, links on the right (`justify-content: space-between`, `align-items: center`).
2. A row of three feature cards that wrap on small screens (`flex-wrap: wrap`, `flex: 1 1 200px`, `gap`).
3. A "hero" box whose text is perfectly centered horizontally and vertically.
4. Make the page footer stay at the bottom using a column flex layout on `body`.
5. Resize the preview window and watch the cards wrap.

lessons.title: CSS Grid layout
lessons.summary: Build two-dimensional layouts with grid columns, rows, gaps, fr units and named areas.

slides.title: Rows and columns together
slides.text: `display: grid` + `grid-template-columns` creates a **2D** layout.
slides.narration:
CSS grid is built for two dimensional layouts, rows and columns at the same time.
Set display grid on the container and describe the columns. Here we get three equal columns with a gap between every cell.

slides.title: The fr unit and repeat()
slides.text:
`fr` = a **fraction** of the free space.
`repeat(4, 1fr)` = four equal columns.
slides.narration:
The f r unit means a fraction of the remaining space. Two f r and one f r split the space two thirds and one third.
repeat saves typing when many columns are the same.

slides.title: Auto-fit responsive grid
slides.text: The famous one-liner: as many columns as fit, each at least 200px.
slides.narration:
This single line creates a responsive grid without any media queries.
minmax says each column is at least two hundred pixels and at most one fraction. auto fit creates as many columns as fit in the container.

slides.title: Placing items
slides.text: Items can span lines: `grid-column: 1 / 3` or `span 2`.
slides.narration:
Items flow into cells automatically, but you can place or stretch them. grid column one slash three runs from line one to line three, covering two columns.
span two is a shorter way to say it, and one slash minus one stretches across the whole row.

slides.title: Named areas
slides.text: Draw your layout with **names**.
slides.narration:
Named areas let you draw the layout as a little text map.
Each string is a row, and each word is a cell. Then assign elements to areas with grid area. Changing the layout later is as simple as redrawing the map.

quiz.q: What does 1fr mean?
options: One fraction of the free space
quiz.explain: fr distributes the remaining space in fractions.

quiz.q: What does grid-column: 1 / -1 do?
options: Spans from the first to the last line (full width)
quiz.explain: -1 refers to the last grid line, so the item spans all columns.

quiz.q: Which is a responsive grid without media queries?
quiz.explain: auto-fit with minmax creates as many columns as fit.

lessons.task:
Build a magazine-style page with grid:

1. Use `grid-template-areas` for header, sidebar, main and footer.
2. Inside main, create a photo gallery with `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr))` and a `gap`.
3. Make one gallery item span two columns and another span two rows.
4. Add a full-width banner using `grid-column: 1 / -1`.
5. Use flexbox inside the header for the navigation links.

lessons.title: Responsive design
lessons.summary: Make pages that work on phones, tablets and desktops with fluid layouts, media queries and responsive images.

slides.title: One page, every screen
slides.text:
**Responsive design**: the layout **adapts** to the screen size.
Start with the viewport meta tag!
slides.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
slides.narration:
People visit your site on phones, tablets, laptops and huge monitors. Responsive design means one page that adapts to all of them.
It starts with the viewport meta tag. Without it, phones pretend to be desktop screens and shrink your page to a tiny size.

slides.title: Fluid by default
slides.text:
- Use `%`, `fr`, `max-width` instead of fixed widths
- Images: `max-width: 100%; height: auto;`
slides.narration:
The best responsive layouts are fluid from the start. Avoid fixed pixel widths for containers.
Images with max width one hundred percent never overflow their parent. And the min function gives a container that fills small screens but stops growing on big ones.

slides.title: Media queries
slides.text: Apply CSS only when a condition is true.
slides.narration:
A media query wraps rules that apply only under certain conditions, most often a minimum width.
Here the grid has one column on phones, two columns from seven hundred pixels, and three on large screens.

slides.title: Mobile first
slides.text: Write the **phone** styles first, then add `min-width` queries for larger screens.
slides.narration:
Mobile first is the recommended approach. Your base CSS is for small screens, where the layout is simple.
Then you add complexity with min width media queries as space grows. The result is usually less code and faster phones.

slides.title: More responsive tools
slides.text:
- `clamp()` fluid font sizes
- Container queries `@container`
- `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`
- `srcset` / `<picture>` for images
slides.narration:
Modern CSS has even more tools. clamp gives text that scales smoothly between a minimum and a maximum.
Container queries react to the size of a component's container instead of the whole screen. And media features let you respect user preferences like dark mode and reduced motion.

quiz.q: What does the viewport meta tag do?
options: Makes mobile browsers use the real device width
quiz.explain: Without it, phones render the page at a desktop width and shrink it.

quiz.q: In mobile-first CSS, which media queries do you mostly write?
quiz.explain: Base styles target small screens; min-width queries add layout for larger ones.

quiz.q: Which rule keeps images from overflowing their container?
quiz.explain: max-width: 100% lets images shrink with their container.

lessons.task:
Make your site responsive, mobile first:

1. Confirm every page has the viewport meta tag.
2. Write base styles for phones: single column, readable font size, full-width images.
3. Add a `min-width` media query that turns the navigation into a row and the content into two columns.
4. Add a second breakpoint for large screens and limit the content width with `min()` or `max-width`.
5. Use `clamp()` for the main heading and add a `prefers-color-scheme: dark` theme.

lessons.title: Accessibility and best practices
lessons.summary: Build pages everyone can use: keyboard access, alt text, contrast, ARIA basics, and a final checklist.

slides.title: Why accessibility?
slides.text:
Over **1 billion** people live with a disability.
Accessible sites work better for **everyone**, and are often required by law.
slides.narration:
Accessibility, often shortened to a eleven y, means people can use your site whatever their abilities: blind users with screen readers, people who only use a keyboard, people with low vision or color blindness.
It also helps everyone else, like someone reading a phone in bright sunlight. In many countries it is a legal requirement.

slides.title: Semantic HTML first
slides.text:
The best accessibility tool is **correct HTML**:
real `<button>`, `<a>`, `<label>`, headings and landmarks.
slides.code: Save
slides.narration:
Most accessibility comes for free if you use the right elements.
A real button can be reached with the Tab key, pressed with Enter or Space, and is announced as a button. A div does none of that.

slides.title: Keyboard and focus
slides.text:
- Everything must work with **Tab**, **Enter**, **Space**
- Never remove the focus outline without a replacement
- Add a "Skip to content" link
slides.narration:
Put your mouse away and try your site with only the keyboard. Can you reach every link and control? Can you see where you are?
Keep a clear focus style, and add a skip link so keyboard users can jump past the navigation.

slides.title: Text alternatives and contrast
slides.text:
- Meaningful `alt` text, empty `alt=""` for decoration
- Contrast at least **4.5:1** for normal text
- Never rely on **color alone**
slides.code: ⚠ Error: email is required
slides.narration:
Give every meaningful image a useful alt text, and decorative images an empty alt.
Make sure text has enough contrast with its background. And never use color as the only signal, like a red border alone for an error. Add an icon or text too.

slides.title: ARIA: use with care
slides.text:
**ARIA** adds roles and labels when HTML is not enough.
Rule #1: if a native element exists, **use it** instead.
slides.code:
...

8+ characters

Saved!
slides.narration:
ARIA attributes give extra information to assistive technology, for example a label for an icon only button, or a live region that announces updates.
But the first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA when a native HTML element does the job. Wrong ARIA is worse than none.

slides.title: Final checklist
slides.text:
- Valid, semantic HTML with `lang`
- Logical headings, landmarks, labels
- Keyboard-friendly with visible focus
- Alt text, contrast, no color-only info
- Responsive, zoomable to 200%
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`
slides.narration:
Congratulations on reaching the end of the course. Keep this checklist close whenever you build a page.
Semantic structure, keyboard access, text alternatives, good contrast and responsive layouts. If you follow it, your pages will be professional, fast, and usable by everyone.

lessons.notes: ## The POUR principles (WCAG) The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2) say content must be: - **Perceivable**: text alternatives, captions, enough contrast. - **Operable**: keyboard access, enough time, no seizure-inducing flashes. - **Understandable**: clear language, predictable navigation, helpful error messages. - **Robust**: valid HTML that works with assistive technologies. ## Practical rules 1. quiz.q: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: Prefer native HTML elements when they exist
quiz.explain: Native elements come with built-in semantics and keyboard support.

quiz.q: What alt text should a purely decorative image have?
quiz.explain: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image.

quiz.q: What minimum contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal text?
quiz.explain: Normal-size text needs at least 4.5:1.

lessons.task:
Final project: audit and improve your site.

1. Navigate every page using only the keyboard; fix anything you cannot reach or see.
2. Add a skip link and a clear `:focus-visible` style.
3. Check every image's `alt`, every form `label` and the heading order.
4. Check text contrast with a contrast checker and fix anything under 4.5:1.
5. Run the Lighthouse accessibility audit in browser dev tools and fix the issues it lists. Write down three things you improved.
